and show that the replacement preserves all of the relevant algebra while repairing four distinct
defects of the sharp cutoff. Algebraically we establish the modulation/translation identity --- the
Weyl commutation relation $M_bT_a=\chi(ab)T_aM_b$ with $\chi(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$ --- in three
registers: as an operator identity on functions $\R\to\C$; as the defining relation of a
circle-valued Heisenberg group admitting a \emph{faithful} Schr\"odinger representation
$(a,b,z)\mapsto z\,T_aM_b$, with the Gaussian as a separating test vector; and as an identity for
discrete spectral data under joint translation of ordinates and modulation of amplitudes.
Analytically we quantify why the Gaussian is preferable: the rectangular transfer function
$\sin(2\pi T\xi)/(\pi\xi)$ has sidelobe peaks of exact height $4T/(\pi(2n+1))$ at
$\xi_n=(2n+1)/(4T)$, hence a scale-invariant normalised amplitude
$\xi_n|\widehat{w}(\xi_n)|=1/\pi$ and non-summable spurious energy, whereas the Gaussian Gabor
atom has transfer modulus $s\,g_{1/s}(\xi-b)$: strictly unimodal, strictly monotone in
$|\xi-b|$, decaying faster than every power, and summable along the very frequencies at which the
rectangular window leaks. Downstream, the Gaussian-windowed harmonic statistic of a nonempty
conjugate-paired family is strictly positive at every width (no false nulls), continuous and
strictly monotone in the width with the unwindowed statistic as its wide-window limit, admits a
closed-form two-ordinate Rayleigh criterion from the factorisation
$(1-u)(w_1-u(1+u+u^2)w_2)$, and --- via the explicit Schwartz bound
$(t^2)^ng_s(t)\le(s^2/\pi)^nn!$ --- converges on infinite ordinate families for which the
unwindowed statistic diverges.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem with sharp cutoffs}

Let a \emph{spectral family} be a multiset of real ordinates $t$, each carrying an amplitude. In
the motivating setting the ordinates are heights of zeros $\rho=\tfrac12\pm it$ on a critical
line and the amplitudes are the reciprocals $1/\rho$; the quantity of interest is the
multiplicity-sensitive harmonic sum $H(Z)=\sum_{\rho\in Z}1/\rho$, and the computable
approximation is the finite-cutoff sum
\[
  \mathcal{S}_T(Z)=\sum_{\substack{\rho\in Z\\ |\operatorname{Im}\rho|\le T}}\frac1\rho .
\]
The cutoff is an act of windowing whether one acknowledges it or not: it is the windowed sum
$\sum_\rho w(\operatorname{Im}\rho)/\rho$ with $w=\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}$. Once acknowledged, $w$ becomes a
free parameter, and the question is which $w$ is best.

Sharp windows are bad windows because of \emph{spectral leakage}: the transfer function
$\widehat w$ of a discontinuous window has heavy oscillatory tails that inject energy from distant
frequencies into any local measurement. This paper makes that folklore into a precise chain of
theorems, and shows that nothing algebraic is lost in the replacement.

\subsection{What must be preserved}

A window is slid along the axis and tuned to a frequency. The commutation relation of those two
motions is the algebraic backbone of time--frequency analysis, and any proposed window must
interact with them exactly. Section~\ref{sec:heis} shows the relation is a group law: the
Heisenberg group, acting faithfully, with the Gaussian as a test vector strong enough to prove
faithfulness single-handedly.

\section{Translation, modulation, and the Heisenberg group}\label{sec:heis}

\subsection{The character}

\begin{definition}
For $x\in\R$ set $\chi(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:chi}
$\chi(0)=1$, $\chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)$, $|\chi(x)|=1$, $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$, and
$\chi(x)=1\iff x\in\Z$. In particular $\chi(1/4)=i\ne1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Additivity is the exponential law. The kernel computation is the characterisation
$e^z=1\iff z\in2\pi i\Z$, applied after cancelling $i$ and dividing by $2\pi$. Finally $4n=1$ has
no integer solution.
\end{proof}

The quarter-period fact $\chi(1/4)\ne1$ is load-bearing: it is the separating input both in the
non-removability of the Weyl phase and in faithfulness.

\subsection{The two motions}

\begin{definition}
For $a,b\in\R$ and $f:\R\to\C$ set
\[
  (T_af)(t)=f(t-a),\qquad (M_bf)(t)=\chi(bt)f(t)=e^{2\pi ibt}f(t).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$T_0=M_0=\mathrm{id}$, $T_aT_{a'}=T_{a+a'}$, $M_bM_{b'}=M_{b+b'}$, and both families are
$\C$-linear in the window.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{The Weyl commutation relation}

\begin{theorem}[Modulation/translation identity]\label{thm:weyl}
For all $a,b\in\R$ and all $f:\R\to\C$,
\[
  M_bT_af=\chi(ab)\,T_aM_bf .
\]
Equivalently $T_aM_bf=\chi(-ab)M_bT_af$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Evaluate at $t$: the left side is $\chi(bt)f(t-a)$, the right side
$\chi(ba)\chi(b(t-a))f(t-a)$, and $\chi(ba)\chi(bt-ba)=\chi(bt)$ by additivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The phase is not removable]\label{thm:notriv}
If $f(0)\ne0$ then $M_{1/2}T_{1/2}f\ne T_{1/2}M_{1/2}f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
At $t=1/2$ the two sides are $\chi(1/4)f(0)$ and $f(0)$; equality would force $\chi(1/4)=1$,
contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:chi}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Heisenberg group}

\begin{definition}
Let $\Heis$ be the set of triples $(a,b,z)$ with $a,b\in\R$ and $z$ on the unit circle, with
\[
  (a,b,z)\cdot(a',b',z')=\bigl(a+a',\,b+b',\,zz'\chi(ba')\bigr),
\]
unit $(0,0,1)$ and inverse $(a,b,z)^{-1}=(-a,-b,z^{-1}\chi(ba))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
$\Heis$ is a group.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
All axioms reduce to the phase coordinate. Associativity is the $2$-cocycle identity
$ba'+(b+b')a''=b'a''+b(a'+a'')$, a polynomial identity; the unit and inverse axioms reduce to
$\chi(ba)\chi(-ba)=1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Schr\"odinger (Gabor) representation}

\begin{definition}
For $g=(a,b,z)\in\Heis$ set $\pi(g)f=z\,T_aM_bf$, i.e.
$(\pi(g)f)(t)=z\,\chi\bigl(b(t-a)\bigr)f(t-a)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Representation property]\label{thm:rep}
$\pi(1)=\mathrm{id}$ and $\pi(gh)=\pi(g)\pi(h)$; each $\pi(g)$ is invertible with inverse
$\pi(g^{-1})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expanding at $t$ and using additivity of $\chi$,
\[
  \chi\bigl((b+b')(t-a-a')\bigr)=\chi\bigl(b(t-a)\bigr)\chi\bigl(b'((t-a)-a')\bigr)\chi(ba')^{-1},
\]
and the leftover $\chi(ba')$ is exactly the cocycle inserted in the group law.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Faithfulness]\label{thm:faithful}
$\pi$ is injective. Indeed if $\pi(g)$ fixes the single Gaussian $\gamma(t)=e^{-t^2}$ then $g=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $g=(a,b,z)$. Taking absolute values kills $z$ and $\chi$ and leaves
$e^{-(t-a)^2}=e^{-t^2}$; evaluating at $t=0$ and $t=a$ gives $a^2=0$, so $a=0$. The identity then
reads $z\chi(bt)\gamma(t)=\gamma(t)$ with $\gamma$ nowhere zero, so $z\chi(bt)=1$ for all $t$; at
$t=0$, $z=1$. If $b\ne0$, taking $t=1/(4b)$ gives $\chi(1/4)=1$, contradicting
Lemma~\ref{lem:chi}.
\end{proof}

Consequently the central circle factor is not redundant: the Weyl cocycle is not a coboundary, and
no rescaling of the operators $T_aM_b$ produces an honest representation of $\R^2$. A single
Gaussian suffices as a test vector.

\section{The Gaussian window and Fourier self-duality}

\begin{definition}
For $s>0$ the \emph{Gaussian window} of width $s$ is $g_s(t)=e^{-\pi t^2/s^2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:gauss}
$g_s>0$, $g_s(0)=1$, $g_s$ is even, $g_s\le1$, and $g_s(t)<1$ for $t\ne0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Closure under products of translates]
For $s\ne0$,
\[
  g_s(t-a)\,g_s(t-b)=e^{-\pi(a-b)^2/(2s^2)}\;g_{s/\sqrt2}\!\left(t-\frac{a+b}{2}\right).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The polarisation identity
$(t-a)^2+(t-b)^2=2\bigl(t-\tfrac{a+b}2\bigr)^2+\tfrac{(a-b)^2}2$, exponentiated.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Rapid decay]\label{lem:rapid}
For $s>0$ and every $n\in\N$, $t^ng_s(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$.
\end{lemma}

We use the normalisation $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_\R e^{-2\pi i\xi t}f(t)\,dt$.

\begin{theorem}[Intertwining]\label{thm:intertwine}
For all $a,b,\xi$ and all $f$,
\[
  \widehat{T_af}(\xi)=\chi(-a\xi)\widehat f(\xi),\qquad
  \widehat{M_bf}(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi-b)=\bigl(T_b\widehat f\bigr)(\xi).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Changes of variable inside the defining integral: translation invariance of Lebesgue measure
produces the constant phase $\chi(-a\xi)$; the extra factor $\chi(bt)$ merges with
$e^{-2\pi i\xi t}$ into $e^{-2\pi i(\xi-b)t}$. Both are equalities of integrals of
pointwise-equal integrands, so no integrability hypotheses are needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Self-duality with width inversion]\label{thm:selfdual}
For $s>0$, $\widehat{g_s}=s\,g_{1/s}$, i.e. $\widehat{g_s}(\xi)=s\,e^{-\pi s^2\xi^2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $g_s(t)=e^{-\pi bt^2}$ with $b=1/s^2>0$ and use
$\widehat{e^{-\pi bt^2}}=b^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/b}$, identifying $b^{-1/2}$ with the positive real
square root $s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{Gabor atom} at phase-space point $(a,b)$ with width $s$ is
$\gamma_{s,a,b}=T_aM_bg_s$, i.e. $\gamma_{s,a,b}(t)=\chi\bigl(b(t-a)\bigr)g_s(t-a)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Heisenberg covariance]\label{thm:cov}
For $g=(a_0,b_0,z_0)\in\Heis$,
$\pi(g)\gamma_{s,a,b}=z_0\chi(b_0a)\,\gamma_{s,\,a_0+a,\;b_0+b}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Transfer function of a Gabor atom]\label{thm:atomtransfer}
For $s>0$,
\[
  \widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\xi)=\chi(-a\xi)\,s\,g_{1/s}(\xi-b),\qquad
  \bigl|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\xi)\bigr|=s\,g_{1/s}(\xi-b).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Strict unimodality; no sidelobes]\label{cor:unimodal}
For $s>0$ and $\xi\ne b$, $|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\xi)|<|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(b)|=s$;
and if $|\xi-b|<|\eta-b|$ then
$|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\eta)|<|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\xi)|$.
\end{corollary}

\section{The Dirichlet kernel: exact sidelobes of the sharp cutoff}

\begin{theorem}[Dirichlet transfer function]\label{thm:dirichlet}
For $T\ge0$ and $\xi\ne0$,
\[
  \widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi)=\frac{\sin(2\pi T\xi)}{\pi\xi},\qquad
  \bigl|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi)\bigr|=\frac{|\sin(2\pi T\xi)|}{\pi|\xi|}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\int_{-T}^{T}e^{-2\pi i\xi t}dt=\bigl(e^{-2\pi i\xi T}-e^{2\pi i\xi T}\bigr)/(-2\pi i\xi)$, and
Euler's formula converts this to $\sin(2\pi T\xi)/(\pi\xi)$. At $\xi=0$ the value is $2T$, so the
hypothesis $\xi\ne0$ is essential.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The $n$-th \emph{sidelobe frequency} of the window of half-width $T>0$ is
$\xi_n=(2n+1)/(4T)$, at which $|\sin(2\pi T\xi_n)|=|\sin((2n+1)\pi/2)|=1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact peak heights]\label{thm:peaks}
For $T>0$ and all $n$, $\bigl|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi_n)\bigr|=\dfrac{4T}{\pi(2n+1)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scale-invariant leakage]\label{thm:leak}
For $T>0$ and all $n$, $\;\xi_n\cdot\bigl|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi_n)\bigr|=\dfrac1\pi$.
\end{theorem}

The constant $1/\pi$ depends on neither $n$ nor $T$: this is the quantitative core of the case
against sharp cutoffs.

\begin{theorem}[Leakage is not negligible]
For $T>0$, $\xi\mapsto\xi\,|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi)|$ does not tend to $0$ as
$\xi\to+\infty$; in particular no bound $|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi)|=o(1/\xi)$ holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Infinite spurious energy]\label{thm:notsummable}
For $T>0$ the sidelobe amplitudes $\bigl(|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi_n)|\bigr)_{n\ge0}$ are not
summable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rapid decay of the Gaussian transfer function]\label{thm:gaussrapid}
For $s>0$, any $a$, and every $n\in\N$, $\;\xi^n|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,0}}(\xi)|\to0$ as
$\xi\to+\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sidelobe suppression]\label{thm:suppress}
For all $T,s>0$ and any $a$, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
  \bigl|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,0}}(\xi_n)\bigr|<\bigl|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi_n)\bigr| .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussrapid} with $n=1$, $\xi|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,0}}(\xi)|\to0$, so
eventually along $\xi_n\to\infty$ it is $<1/\pi$, whereas the rectangular quantity is exactly
$1/\pi$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:leak}. Divide by $\xi_n>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite spurious energy of the Gaussian]\label{thm:gausssummable}
For all $T,s>0$ and any $a$, $\bigl(|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,0}}(\xi_n)|\bigr)_{n\ge0}$ is summable.
\end{theorem}

Thus the windows are separated by three inequivalent criteria: strict unimodality
(Corollary~\ref{cor:unimodal}), rapid decay (Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussrapid}), and summability of
peak amplitudes (Theorems~\ref{thm:notsummable} and~\ref{thm:gausssummable}). The rectangular
window fails all three; the Gaussian satisfies all three.

\section{Windowed spectral statistics and the discrete Weyl identity}

\begin{definition}
For a window $w:\R\to\C$ and a multiset $Z$ of nonzero complex numbers, the \emph{windowed
harmonic sum} is $S_w(Z)=\sum_{\rho\in Z}w(\operatorname{Im}\rho)/\rho$, counted with
multiplicity. It is additive in $Z$ and linear in $w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[The sharp cutoff is the rectangular case]
$S_{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(Z)=\sum_{\rho\in Z,\ |\operatorname{Im}\rho|\le T}\rho^{-1}$.
\end{proposition}

Let $P(S)$ denote the conjugate-paired family $\{\tfrac12\pm it: t\in S\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Paired collapse under a smooth window]
$S_{g_s}(P(S))=\sum_{t\in S}\dfrac{g_s(t)}{\tfrac14+t^2}\in\R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(\tfrac12+it)^{-1}+(\tfrac12-it)^{-1}=1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$, and $g_s$ is real and even, so the
window factor is common to the pair.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict positivity; no false nulls]\label{thm:nonull}
If $S\ne\varnothing$ then $\operatorname{Re}S_{g_s}(P(S))>0$ for every width $s$. Consequently
$S_{g_s}(P(S))=0$ iff $S=\varnothing$, for every $s\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The sharp contrast]
If $|t|>T$ then the sharp cutoff of half-width $T$ returns $0$ on $P(\{t\})$, while the Gaussian
statistic of any width returns a strictly positive value.
\end{theorem}

What removes false nulls is strict positivity of the window on the whole line; what removes
sidelobes is smoothness. These are independent defects of the sharp cutoff, and the Gaussian
repairs both.

\begin{definition}
\emph{Spectral data} is a multiset $D=\{(t_j,c_j)\}\subset\R\times\C$. The \emph{discrete Gabor
transform} of $D$ with window $w$ at the phase-space point $(a,b)$ is
\[
  G_w(D)(a,b)=\sum_j\chi(-bt_j)\,w(t_j-a)\,c_j .
\]
\end{definition}

At the origin of phase space $G_w(D)(0,0)=S_w(Z)$ for the data of a zero multiset $Z$: the
transform extends the windowed sum.

\begin{theorem}[Translation and modulation]\label{thm:transmod}
Writing $D+c$ for the data with ordinates shifted by $c$ and $D^{(\eta)}$ for the data with
amplitudes multiplied by $\chi(\eta t_j)$,
\[
  G_w(D+c)(a,b)=\chi(-bc)\,G_w(D)(a-c,b),\qquad
  G_w\bigl(D^{(\eta)}\bigr)(a,b)=G_w(D)(a,b-\eta).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Weyl identity for spectral data]\label{thm:discweyl}
For all $a,b,c,\eta$,
\[
  G_w\bigl(D^{(\eta)}+c\bigr)(a,b)=\chi(-\eta c)\,G_w\bigl((D+c)^{(\eta)}\bigr)(a,b).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:transmod} in the two orders: one produces the phase $\chi(-bc)$, the other
$\chi(-(b-\eta)c)$, at the same analysis point $(a-c,b-\eta)$. The ratio is $\chi(-\eta c)$.
\end{proof}

This is the operator-level Weyl relation transported verbatim to discrete data.

\section{Scale space: the width as a continuous parameter}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{Gaussian spectral profile} of a family $S$ is
$\Sigma(S,s)=\sum_{t\in S}g_s(t)/(\tfrac14+t^2)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotone scale space]\label{thm:mono}
If $0<s_1\le s_2$ then $\Sigma(S,s_1)\le\Sigma(S,s_2)$; if moreover $s_1<s_2$ and $S$ contains
some $t\ne0$, the inequality is strict.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Continuity]
$s\mapsto\Sigma(S,s)$ is continuous on $\{s\ne0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The sharp cutoff is discontinuous]
For a single conjugate pair with ordinate $t$, the map
$T\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\mathcal{S}_T(P(\{t\}))$ is not continuous at $T=|t|$: it
equals $0$ for $T<|t|$ and $1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$ at $T=|t|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Wide-window limit]\label{thm:widelimit}
For every finite family $S$, $\;\lim_{s\to\infty}\Sigma(S,s)=\sum_{t\in S}1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$, the
unwindowed harmonic statistic of the paired family.
\end{theorem}

The Gaussian statistic is therefore a deformation of the classical one, running continuously and
strictly monotonically from ``see nothing'' at $s\to0$ to ``see everything'' at $s\to\infty$.

\section{Peak localisation and a Rayleigh criterion}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{position profile} of $S$ at width $s$ is
$P_S(a)=\sum_{t\in S}g_s(t-a)/(\tfrac14+t^2)$; it is the real part of the discrete Gabor
transform of the paired data at frequency $0$, and $P_S(0)=\Sigma(S,s)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Unbiased localisation]
For a single ordinate $t$ and $s\ne0$, $P_{\{t\}}(a)<P_{\{t\}}(t)$ for all $a\ne t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Scale doubling]\label{lem:scaledouble}
For all $s,d$: $\;g_s(d/2)=g_{2s}(d)$ and $g_s(d)=g_{2s}(d)^4$.
\end{lemma}

Fix $t_1\ne t_2$ and set $u=g_{2s}(t_1-t_2)\in(0,1)$ and $w_i=1/(\tfrac14+t_i^2)>0$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact profile values]
For $S=\{t_1,t_2\}$: $\;P_S(t_1)=w_1+u^4w_2$ and
$P_S\bigl(\tfrac{t_1+t_2}2\bigr)=u(w_1+w_2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp resolution criterion]\label{thm:sharpres}
\[
  P_S(t_1)-P_S\!\left(\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}\right)=(1-u)\bigl(w_1-u(1+u+u^2)w_2\bigr),
\]
so the midpoint lies strictly below the peak at $t_1$ if and only if $u(1+u+u^2)w_2<w_1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Subtract and factor $(1-u)w_1-u(1-u^3)w_2$ using $1-u^3=(1-u)(1+u+u^2)$; since $t_1\ne t_2$ we
have $u<1$, so the first factor is positive.
\end{proof}

The factorisation separates the failure modes: $1-u$ vanishes exactly for coincident ordinates,
while the second factor is the genuine resolution threshold.

\begin{theorem}[Rayleigh criterion]\label{thm:rayleigh}
Let $s>0$ and $t_1\ne t_2$. If
$\;3\,g_{2s}(t_1-t_2)\bigl(\tfrac14+t_1^2\bigr)\le\tfrac14+t_2^2$, then
$P_S\bigl(\tfrac{t_1+t_2}2\bigr)<P_S(t_1)$: the ordinates are resolved and the midpoint is a
valley, not a spurious peak.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Never vacuous]\label{thm:nevervac}
For any $t_1\ne t_2$, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:rayleigh} holds for all sufficiently
small $s>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For fixed $d=t_1-t_2\ne0$, $g_{2s}(d)=e^{-\pi d^2/(4s^2)}\to0$ as $s\downarrow0$, while the
right-hand side is a fixed positive constant.
\end{proof}

For example $t_1=14.13$, $t_2=21.02$, $s=4$ give $u\approx0.0974$, $w_1\approx0.00500$,
$w_2\approx0.00226$, and $3uw_2\le w_1$ reads $0.00066\le0.00500$: comfortably resolved. Narrowing
a Gaussian always eventually separates distinct ordinates; narrowing a rectangle never removes its
$1/\pi$ leakage floor.

\section{Schwartz decay and Gaussian regularisation}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit Schwartz bound]\label{thm:schwartz}
For $s\ne0$, every $n\in\N$ and every $t$,
\[
  (t^2)^n\,g_s(t)\le\left(\frac{s^2}{\pi}\right)^{\!n}n! .
\]
Consequently $g_s(t)\le(s^2/\pi)^nn!/(t^2)^n$ for $t\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $y=\pi t^2/s^2\ge0$, so $g_s(t)=e^{-y}$ and $t^2=(s^2/\pi)y$; the inequality $y^n/n!\le e^y$
gives $y^ne^{-y}\le n!$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrary powers]
For $s\ne0$, every $m\in\N$ and every $t$,
$\;|t|^mg_s(t)\le1+\left(s^2/\pi\right)^{m}m!$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
The additive $1$ cannot be dropped: $|t|^mg_s(t)$ is maximised at $|t|=s\sqrt{m/2\pi}$, and for
$m=1$, $s=1/2$ the maximum is $\approx0.12099$ while $(s^2/\pi)^1\cdot1!\approx0.07958$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform decay over the Heisenberg orbit]
For $s\ne0$, every $m$ and every phase-space point $(a,b)$,
\[
  |t-a|^m\bigl|\gamma_{s,a,b}(t)\bigr|\le1+\left(\frac{s^2}{\pi}\right)^{\!m}m!\qquad\text{for all }t,
\]
with a constant independent of $(a,b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian regularisation]\label{thm:regularise}
Let $s\ne0$ and let $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ satisfy the square-root growth condition $k+1\le t_k^2$. Then
$\sum_{k\ge0}g_s(t_k)/(\tfrac14+t_k^2)<\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $M=(s^2/\pi)^2\cdot2!$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:schwartz} at $n=2$,
$g_s(t_k)/(\tfrac14+t_k^2)\le4g_s(t_k)\le4M/(t_k^2)^2\le4M/(k+1)^2$, which is summable.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness at the threshold]\label{thm:sharpthresh}
For $t_k=\sqrt{k+1}$, which satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:regularise} with
equality, the unwindowed series diverges:
$\sum_{k\ge0}1/(\tfrac14+t_k^2)=\sum_{k\ge0}1/(k+\tfrac54)=\infty$.
\end{theorem}

On this family the Gaussian window converts a divergent statistic into a convergent one; no window
bounded below by a positive constant can do this. The mechanism is a quantifier order: the
constant $C_n=(s^2/\pi)^nn!$ grows with $n$ but is independent of $t$, so the order may be chosen
after seeing the growth exponent of the family. Numerically, with $s=1$,
$\sum_{k<10^4}1/(k+\tfrac54)\approx9.4379$ and still growing like $\log k$, whereas
$\sum_{k<10^4}g_1(t_k)/(k+\tfrac54)\approx0.035427$, constant to five digits past $k=3$.

\section{Algorithms and applications}

The results assemble into a peak-finding pipeline for spectral data $D=\{(t_j,c_j)\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Choose a width.} Compute the scale space $s\mapsto\Sigma(S,s)$; by
    Theorem~\ref{thm:mono} it is continuous and strictly increasing, and its knee identifies the
    scale at which the family's mass is captured.
  \item \textbf{Slide.} Evaluate $P_S(a)$ on a grid --- the discrete Gabor transform at frequency
    $0$. Cost $O(|D|\cdot|\mathrm{grid}|)$, or $O(N\log N)$ per frequency slice for gridded data.
  \item \textbf{Detect.} Report local maxima; these are unbiased for isolated ordinates, and by
    Corollary~\ref{cor:unimodal} none can be an artefact of the window's transfer function.
  \item \textbf{Certify resolution.} For adjacent detected peaks check the criterion of
    Theorem~\ref{thm:rayleigh}; if it fails, narrow $s$, which succeeds eventually by
    Theorem~\ref{thm:nevervac}.
  \item \textbf{Move in phase space.} To analyse at frequency $b$ use $\gamma_{s,a,b}$; the
    bookkeeping is exact by Theorem~\ref{thm:cov}, and shifted or modulated data must carry the
    phase $\chi(-\eta c)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:discweyl}.
\end{enumerate}
Step 4 is what a rectangular pipeline cannot supply: its leakage floor $1/\pi$ is
width-independent.

For infinite families whose classical statistic diverges, Theorem~\ref{thm:regularise} supplies a
convergent surrogate at each width and Theorem~\ref{thm:widelimit} recovers the classical value on
finite families as $s\to\infty$, giving a principled regularisation with lower brackets from
monotonicity.

Nothing in the operator algebra, the transfer-function comparison, or the Schwartz bounds refers
to the specific amplitudes $1/\rho$; those sections apply to any windowed analysis of point data.

\section{Discussion and limitations}

All strictness statements carry $s\ne0$ (or $s>0$); at $s=0$ the formula $e^{-\pi t^2/s^2}$
degenerates. The constant $3$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:rayleigh} is a convenient weakening of the sharp
Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpres}, costing at most a factor $3$ in the overlap variable. The resolution
analysis is complete for pairs only; for three or more nearby ordinates the profile difference is
no longer a product of two factors in one variable. Sections on statistics concern finite
multisets except for the regularisation theorem. Theorem~\ref{thm:sharpthresh} is about the
specific threshold family $\sqrt{k+1}$: the point is the existence of a threshold at which the two
windows disagree about whether the statistic exists, not a blanket claim. Finally, the convention
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi t}f(t)dt$ makes the self-duality clean and the character have
integer kernel; other conventions rescale constants but change nothing structural.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Gaussian extremality of the discrete uncertainty product]
For the discrete Gabor transform define the position spread $\Delta a(w)^2$ and frequency spread
$\Delta\xi(w)^2$ of a normalised window $w$. Then $\Delta a(w)\Delta\xi(w)\ge1/(4\pi)$, with
equality iff $w$ is a Gaussian $g_s$ up to the Heisenberg action --- i.e. the orbit of the
Gaussian is exactly the equality locus.
\end{conjecture}

Self-duality already exhibits the Gaussian as the unique fixed ray of the Fourier transform inside
the window family, and Theorem~\ref{thm:cov} forces the equality locus to be a full orbit. The
operator half is complete, since the intertwining relations hold with no integrability
hypotheses; the missing ingredient is the second moment
$\int x^2e^{-bx^2}dx=\tfrac1{2b}\sqrt{\pi/b}$.

\begin{conjecture}[Non-summability of spurious energy as a window invariant]
Define the spurious energy of a window as the sum of its transfer function's local-maximum
amplitudes outside the main lobe. This invariant is infinite for the rectangular window and finite
for every Gaussian atom, uniformly over the Heisenberg orbit; conjecturally it is finite exactly
for windows of bounded variation with integrable derivative, and the finite/infinite dichotomy
classifies admissible analysing windows, with the scale-invariance
$\xi_n|\widehat w(\xi_n)|=1/\pi$ as the model obstruction.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions: extend the two-ordinate factorisation to $m\ge3$ ordinates in terms of the
pairwise overlaps $u_{ij}=g_{2s}(t_i-t_j)$; determine the exact growth boundary $t_k^2\sim
\varphi(k)$ separating convergence of the windowed series from divergence of the unwindowed one as
a function of the width; and isolate the minimal hypotheses on a general Schwartz window under
which each of the results above survives.

\section{Conclusion}

Replacing a sharp cutoff by a Gaussian window costs nothing algebraically and gains a great deal
analytically. The modulation/translation identity $M_bT_a=\chi(ab)T_aM_b$ holds exactly, is the
group law of a Heisenberg group, and is realised by a faithful representation for which a single
Gaussian is a separating test vector. The rectangular transfer function leaks a scale-invariant
$1/\pi$ of normalised amplitude at arbitrarily high frequency with non-summable total energy, while
the Gaussian atom's transfer function is a single strictly monotone lobe with faster-than-polynomial
decay and summable spurious response. Downstream this converts a discontinuous, sometimes-blind
statistic into a continuous, strictly monotone scale space with the classical statistic as its
wide-window limit; it makes peak localisation unbiased and equips it with a floor-free resolution
criterion; and it regularises statistics on infinite families for which the classical sum does not
exist. The unifying reason is that the Gaussian is a distinguished vector in a representation of
the Heisenberg group, and every property above is inherited uniformly across its orbit.

import cmath
import math
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Complex = complex
Window = Callable[[float], Complex]

TAU: float = 2.0 * math.pi


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The character and the two motions
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def chi(x: float) -> Complex:
    """The basic additive character chi(x) = exp(2 pi i x)."""
    return cmath.exp(1j * TAU * x)


def translate(a: float, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Translation operator (T_a f)(t) = f(t - a)."""
    return lambda t: f(t - a)


def modulate(b: float, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Modulation operator (M_b f)(t) = chi(b t) f(t)."""
    return lambda t: chi(b * t) * f(t)


def gauss_window(s: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Gaussian window g_s(t) = exp(-pi t^2 / s^2)."""
    return math.exp(-math.pi * t * t / (s * s))


def gauss_c(s: float) -> Window:
    """Complex-valued Gaussian window."""
    return lambda t: complex(gauss_window(s, t), 0.0)


def gabor_atom(s: float, a: float, b: float) -> Window:
    """Gabor atom gamma_{s,a,b} = T_a M_b g_s."""
    return translate(a, modulate(b, gauss_c(s)))


def demo_weyl_relation() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1. THE WEYL COMMUTATION RELATION   M_b T_a = chi(a b) T_a M_b")
    print("=" * 78)
    a, b, s = 0.7, 1.3, 1.5
    f = gauss_c(s)
    left = modulate(b, translate(a, f))
    right = translate(a, modulate(b, f))
    worst = 0.0
    for t in [-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.35, 1.9, 4.0]:
        worst = max(worst, abs(left(t) - chi(a * b) * right(t)))
    print(f"  a = {a}, b = {b}, s = {s}")
    print(f"  max |M_b T_a f(t) - chi(ab) T_a M_b f(t)|  =  {worst:.3e}   (should be ~0)")

    # The phase is not removable: a = b = 1/2, evaluated at t = 1/2, differs by chi(1/4) = i.
    a2 = b2 = 0.5
    lhs = modulate(b2, translate(a2, f))(0.5)
    rhs = translate(a2, modulate(b2, f))(0.5)
    print(f"  a = b = 1/2 at t = 1/2:  lhs = {lhs:.6f},  rhs = {rhs:.6f}")
    print(f"  ratio lhs/rhs = {lhs / rhs:.6f}   (equals chi(1/4) = i, so the orders differ)")

# 2. The Heisenberg group and the Gabor representation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HeisElt = Tuple[float, float, Complex]


def heis_mul(g: HeisElt, h: HeisElt) -> HeisElt:
    """(a,b,z)(a',b',z') = (a+a', b+b', z z' chi(b a'))."""
    a, b, z = g
    a2, b2, z2 = h
    return (a + a2, b + b2, z * z2 * chi(b * a2))


def heis_inv(g: HeisElt) -> HeisElt:
    """Inverse in the Heisenberg group."""
    a, b, z = g
    return (-a, -b, chi(b * a) / z)


def gabor_act(g: HeisElt, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Schroedinger representation pi(a,b,z) f = z T_a M_b f."""
    a, b, z = g
    return lambda t: z * translate(a, modulate(b, f))(t)


def demo_heisenberg() -> None:

    h: HeisElt = (-0.9, 0.6, chi(0.41))
    k: HeisElt = (1.7, 0.25, chi(-0.2))

    left = heis_mul(heis_mul(g, h), k)
    right = heis_mul(g, heis_mul(h, k))
    assoc = max(abs(left[0] - right[0]), abs(left[1] - right[1]), abs(left[2] - right[2]))
    print(f"  associativity residual                 = {assoc:.3e}")

    ident = heis_mul(g, heis_inv(g))

                               - gabor_act(g, gabor_act(h, f))(t)))
    print(f"  representation property  pi(gh) = pi(g)pi(h), residual = {resid:.3e}")

        print(f"  {label}: max deviation on Gaussian = {dev:.4f}   (nonzero => detected)")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rect_transfer(T: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F 1_[-T,T](xi)| = |sin(2 pi T xi)| / (pi |xi|)."""
    if xi == 0.0:
        return 2.0 * T
    return abs(math.sin(TAU * T * xi)) / (math.pi * abs(xi))


def gauss_transfer(s: float, b: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F gamma_{s,a,b}(xi)| = s g_{1/s}(xi - b)  (independent of a)."""
    return s * gauss_window(1.0 / s, xi - b)


def sidelobe_freq(T: float, n: int) -> float:
    """xi_n = (2n+1)/(4T)."""
    return (2.0 * n + 1.0) / (4.0 * T)

        v = gauss_transfer(s, b, xi)
        flag = "" if prev is None else ("  strictly smaller" if v < prev else "  !! NOT monotone")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Windowed statistics, false nulls, and the scale space
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def window_sum_rect(ordinates: Sequence[float], T: float) -> float:
    """Sharp cutoff statistic: sum over |t| <= T of 1/(1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates if abs(t) <= T)


def gauss_spectral(ordinates: Sequence[float], s: float) -> float:
    """Gaussian scale space Sigma(S, s) = sum_t g_s(t) / (1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(gauss_window(s, t) / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


def harmonic_statistic(ordinates: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Unwindowed statistic sum_t 1/(1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


# The first few ordinates of the classical critical-line family, used as realistic data.
ORDINATES: List[float] = [14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062,
                          37.586178, 40.918719, 43.327073, 48.005151, 49.773832]


def demo_scale_space() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5. NO FALSE NULLS, AND THE GAUSSIAN SCALE SPACE")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("  Rectangular cutoff on the first ten ordinates (it jumps, and vanishes early):")
    for T in [5.0, 14.0, 14.134725, 20.0, 21.022040, 100.0]:
        print(f"    T = {T:10.6f}   windowSum = {window_sum_rect(ORDINATES, T):.8f}")
    print()
    print("  Gaussian scale space (continuous, strictly increasing, never zero):")
    prev = None
    for s in [1.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0, 80.0, 200.0, 1000.0]:
        v = gauss_spectral(ORDINATES, s)

        print(f"    s = {s:8.1f}   Sigma = {v:.6e}{mono}")
        prev = v

    print()
    print("  A single ordinate outside the cutoff is invisible to the sharp window:")
    t_far = 21.02204
    print(f"    windowSum({{{t_far}}}, T = 10) = {window_sum_rect([t_far], 10.0):.10f}")
    for s in [10.0, 20.0, 50.0]:
        print(f"    Gaussian statistic, s = {s:4.1f}   = {gauss_spectral([t_far], s):.3e}  (> 0)")
    # For very narrow windows the value is still strictly positive but underflows binary
    # floating point; its base-10 logarithm is computed exactly instead.
    for s in [0.5, 2.0]:
        log10_val = (-math.pi * t_far * t_far / (s * s)) / math.log(10.0) \

        print(f"    Gaussian statistic, s = {s:4.1f}   = 10^({log10_val:.1f})  (> 0, underflows float)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Peak localisation and the Rayleigh criterion
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pos_profile(ordinates: Sequence[float], s: float, a: float) -> float:
    """Position profile P_S(a) = sum_t g_s(t - a) / (1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(gauss_window(s, t - a) / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


def rayleigh_resolved(t1: float, t2: float, s: float) -> bool:
    """Rayleigh criterion 3 g_{2s}(t1 - t2) (1/4 + t1^2) <= 1/4 + t2^2."""
    return 3.0 * gauss_window(2.0 * s, t1 - t2) * (0.25 + t1 * t1) <= 0.25 + t2 * t2


def demo_peaks() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6. PEAK LOCALISATION AND THE RAYLEIGH CRITERION")
    print("=" * 78)
    t1, t2 = 14.134725, 21.022040
    for s in [10.0, 6.0, 4.0, 2.0]:
        u = gauss_window(2.0 * s, t1 - t2)
        w1, w2 = 1.0 / (0.25 + t1 * t1), 1.0 / (0.25 + t2 * t2)
        at_t1 = pos_profile([t1, t2], s, t1)
        at_mid = pos_profile([t1, t2], s, (t1 + t2) / 2.0)
        # Exact values from the scale-doubling identities.
        pred_t1 = w1 + u ** 4 * w2
        pred_mid = u * (w1 + w2)
        # Exact factorisation of the difference.
        factored = (1.0 - u) * (w1 - u * (1.0 + u + u * u) * w2)
        print(f"  s = {s:5.1f}:  u = g_2s(d) = {u:.6f}")
        print(f"      P(t1)      = {at_t1:.10f}   (formula w1 + u^4 w2 = {pred_t1:.10f})")
        print(f"      P(midpoint)= {at_mid:.10f}   (formula u(w1 + w2)  = {pred_mid:.10f})")
        print(f"      difference = {at_t1 - at_mid:.10f}   "
              f"(factorisation (1-u)(w1 - u(1+u+u^2)w2) = {factored:.10f})")
        print(f"      sharp criterion u(1+u+u^2)w2 < w1 : "
              f"{u * (1 + u + u * u) * w2:.3e} < {w1:.3e}  -> "
              f"{'RESOLVED' if u * (1 + u + u * u) * w2 < w1 else 'merged'}")
        print(f"      Rayleigh criterion (constant 3)   : "
              f"{'satisfied' if rayleigh_resolved(t1, t2, s) else 'not satisfied'}")
    print()
    print("  Unbiased localisation for a single ordinate (peak exactly at t):")
    t = 14.134725
    for a in [t - 1.0, t - 0.1, t, t + 0.1, t + 1.0]:
        print(f"    a = {a:11.6f}   P(a) = {pos_profile([t], 3.0, a):.10f}")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Schwartz bounds and regularisation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def schwartz_bound(s: float, n: int) -> float:
    """The explicit constant (s^2/pi)^n n! in (t^2)^n g_s(t) <= (s^2/pi)^n n!."""
    return (s * s / math.pi) ** n * math.factorial(n)


def demo_schwartz() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7. EXPLICIT SCHWARTZ BOUNDS AND GAUSSIAN REGULARISATION")
    print("=" * 78)
    s = 1.0
    print(f"  Checking (t^2)^n g_s(t) <= (s^2/pi)^n n!   for s = {s}:")
    for n in [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]:
        bound = schwartz_bound(s, n)
        worst = max(((t * t) ** n) * gauss_window(s, t)
                    for t in [i * 0.01 for i in range(0, 2001)])
        ok = "ok" if worst <= bound + 1e-9 else "VIOLATED"
        print(f"    n = {n}:  max_t (t^2)^n g_s(t) = {worst:12.6f} <= {bound:12.6f}   [{ok}]")
    print()
    print("  Regularisation on the threshold family t_k = sqrt(k+1):")
    unwindowed = 0.0
    windowed = 0.0
    checkpoints = {3, 10, 100, 1000, 10000}
    for k in range(10000):
        tk2 = float(k + 1)
        unwindowed += 1.0 / (0.25 + tk2)
        windowed += gauss_window(s, math.sqrt(tk2)) / (0.25 + tk2)
        if k + 1 in checkpoints:
            print(f"    k < {k + 1:6d}:  unwindowed = {unwindowed:10.6f}   "
                  f"Gaussian-windowed = {windowed:.8f}")
    print("    the unwindowed partial sums grow like log k (divergent harmonic series),")
    print("    while the Gaussian-windowed sum is constant to five digits past k = 3.")
    print()
    print("  Uniform decay over the Heisenberg orbit, |t-a|^m |gamma_{s,a,b}(t)| <= 1 + (s^2/pi)^m m!:")
    m = 2
    bound = 1.0 + schwartz_bound(s, m)
    worst = 0.0
    for a in [-3.0, 0.0, 1.7]:
        for b in [-2.0, 0.0, 5.0]:
            atom = gabor_atom(s, a, b)
            for i in range(0, 1200):
                t = a - 6.0 + i * 0.01
                worst = max(worst, abs(t - a) ** m * abs(atom(t)))
    print(f"    m = {m}: worst value over a grid of (a, b, t) = {worst:.6f} <= {bound:.6f}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_weyl_relation()
    demo_heisenberg()
    demo_sidelobes()
    demo_scale_space()
    demo_peaks()
    demo_schwartz()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("All demonstrations completed.")
    print("=" * 78)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Self-contained (standard library only) numerical verification of the main results on
Gaussian versus rectangular windows:

  1. The Weyl commutation relation  M_b T_a = chi(a b) T_a M_b, and the fact that the
     phase cannot be removed.
  2. The Heisenberg group law and the Schroedinger (Gabor) representation property,
     including faithfulness on a Gaussian test vector.
  3. Exact sidelobes of the rectangular window: peak height 4T/(pi(2n+1)) at
     xi_n = (2n+1)/(4T), scale-invariant normalised amplitude 1/pi, divergent total energy.
  4. Sidelobe-free Gaussian transfer function |F gamma_{s,a,b}(xi)| = s g_{1/s}(xi - b).
  5. No false nulls, and the continuous, strictly monotone Gaussian scale space with the
     unwindowed harmonic statistic as its wide-window limit.
  6. Peak localisation: the exact profile factorisation and the Rayleigh criterion.
  7. Explicit Schwartz bounds and Gaussian regularisation of a divergent statistic.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Complex = complex
Window = Callable[[float], Complex]

TAU: float = 2.0 * math.pi


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The character and the two motions
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def chi(x: float) -> Complex:
    """The basic additive character chi(x) = exp(2 pi i x)."""
    return cmath.exp(1j * TAU * x)


def translate(a: float, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Translation operator (T_a f)(t) = f(t - a)."""
    return lambda t: f(t - a)


def modulate(b: float, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Modulation operator (M_b f)(t) = chi(b t) f(t)."""
    return lambda t: chi(b * t) * f(t)


def gauss_window(s: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Gaussian window g_s(t) = exp(-pi t^2 / s^2)."""
    return math.exp(-math.pi * t * t / (s * s))


def gauss_c(s: float) -> Window:
    """Complex-valued Gaussian window."""
    return lambda t: complex(gauss_window(s, t), 0.0)


def gabor_atom(s: float, a: float, b: float) -> Window:
    """Gabor atom gamma_{s,a,b} = T_a M_b g_s."""
    return translate(a, modulate(b, gauss_c(s)))


def demo_weyl_relation() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1. THE WEYL COMMUTATION RELATION   M_b T_a = chi(a b) T_a M_b")
    print("=" * 78)
    a, b, s = 0.7, 1.3, 1.5
    f = gauss_c(s)
    left = modulate(b, translate(a, f))
    right = translate(a, modulate(b, f))
    worst = 0.0
    for t in [-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.35, 1.9, 4.0]:
        worst = max(worst, abs(left(t) - chi(a * b) * right(t)))
    print(f"  a = {a}, b = {b}, s = {s}")
    print(f"  max |M_b T_a f(t) - chi(ab) T_a M_b f(t)|  =  {worst:.3e}   (should be ~0)")

    # The phase is not removable: a = b = 1/2, evaluated at t = 1/2, differs by chi(1/4) = i.
    a2 = b2 = 0.5
    lhs = modulate(b2, translate(a2, f))(0.5)
    rhs = translate(a2, modulate(b2, f))(0.5)
    print(f"  a = b = 1/2 at t = 1/2:  lhs = {lhs:.6f},  rhs = {rhs:.6f}")
    print(f"  ratio lhs/rhs = {lhs / rhs:.6f}   (equals chi(1/4) = i, so the orders differ)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The Heisenberg group and the Gabor representation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HeisElt = Tuple[float, float, Complex]


def heis_mul(g: HeisElt, h: HeisElt) -> HeisElt:
    """(a,b,z)(a',b',z') = (a+a', b+b', z z' chi(b a'))."""
    a, b, z = g
    a2, b2, z2 = h
    return (a + a2, b + b2, z * z2 * chi(b * a2))


def heis_inv(g: HeisElt) -> HeisElt:
    """Inverse in the Heisenberg group."""
    a, b, z = g
    return (-a, -b, chi(b * a) / z)


def gabor_act(g: HeisElt, f: Window) -> Window:
    """Schroedinger representation pi(a,b,z) f = z T_a M_b f."""
    a, b, z = g
    return lambda t: z * translate(a, modulate(b, f))(t)


def demo_heisenberg() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("2. HEISENBERG GROUP AND THE FAITHFUL GABOR REPRESENTATION")
    print("=" * 78)
    g: HeisElt = (0.4, -1.1, chi(0.13))
    h: HeisElt = (-0.9, 0.6, chi(0.41))
    k: HeisElt = (1.7, 0.25, chi(-0.2))

    left = heis_mul(heis_mul(g, h), k)
    right = heis_mul(g, heis_mul(h, k))
    assoc = max(abs(left[0] - right[0]), abs(left[1] - right[1]), abs(left[2] - right[2]))
    print(f"  associativity residual                 = {assoc:.3e}")

    ident = heis_mul(g, heis_inv(g))
    print(f"  g g^{-1} = ({ident[0]:.1e}, {ident[1]:.1e}, {ident[2]:.6f})   (should be (0,0,1))")

    f = gauss_c(1.0)
    resid = 0.0
    for t in [-1.5, 0.0, 0.8, 2.2]:
        resid = max(resid, abs(gabor_act(heis_mul(g, h), f)(t)
                               - gabor_act(g, gabor_act(h, f))(t)))
    print(f"  representation property  pi(gh) = pi(g)pi(h), residual = {resid:.3e}")

    # Faithfulness: a nontrivial element moves the Gaussian test vector.
    test: Window = lambda t: complex(math.exp(-t * t), 0.0)
    for elt, label in [((0.3, 0.0, 1 + 0j), "pure translation"),
                       ((0.0, 0.0, chi(0.25)), "pure phase     "),
                       ((0.0, 0.7, 1 + 0j), "pure modulation")]:
        dev = max(abs(gabor_act(elt, test)(t) - test(t)) for t in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0])
        print(f"  {label}: max deviation on Gaussian = {dev:.4f}   (nonzero => detected)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3-4. Transfer functions: Dirichlet sidelobes versus the Gaussian bump
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rect_transfer(T: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F 1_[-T,T](xi)| = |sin(2 pi T xi)| / (pi |xi|)."""
    if xi == 0.0:
        return 2.0 * T
    return abs(math.sin(TAU * T * xi)) / (math.pi * abs(xi))


def gauss_transfer(s: float, b: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F gamma_{s,a,b}(xi)| = s g_{1/s}(xi - b)  (independent of a)."""
    return s * gauss_window(1.0 / s, xi - b)


def sidelobe_freq(T: float, n: int) -> float:
    """xi_n = (2n+1)/(4T)."""
    return (2.0 * n + 1.0) / (4.0 * T)


def demo_sidelobes() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("3-4. SIDELOBES: RECTANGULAR (DIRICHLET) VERSUS GAUSSIAN")
    print("=" * 78)
    T, s = 2.0, 1.0
    print(f"  half-width T = {T}, Gaussian width s = {s}")
    print()
    print("     n     xi_n      |F rect|    xi_n*|F rect|      |F gauss|   ratio g/r")
    print("   " + "-" * 72)
    for n in [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50]:
        xi = sidelobe_freq(T, n)
        r = rect_transfer(T, xi)
        exact = 4.0 * T / (math.pi * (2.0 * n + 1.0))
        assert abs(r - exact) < 1e-12, "exact sidelobe height must match"
        g = gauss_transfer(s, 0.0, xi)
        print(f"   {n:5d} {xi:8.4f}  {r:11.6f}  {xi * r:14.8f}  {g:13.3e}  {g / r:10.2e}")
    print(f"   (the column xi_n*|F rect| is identically 1/pi = {1.0 / math.pi:.8f})")
    print()

    partial_rect = 0.0
    partial_gauss = 0.0
    for n in range(2000):
        xi = sidelobe_freq(T, n)
        partial_rect += rect_transfer(T, xi)
        partial_gauss += gauss_transfer(s, 0.0, xi)
    print(f"  sum of first 2000 rectangular sidelobe peaks = {partial_rect:.4f}  (diverges ~ log N)")
    print(f"  sum of first 2000 Gaussian    responses      = {partial_gauss:.6e}  (converges)")
    print()

    print("  Strict unimodality of the Gaussian transfer function about b = 0.35:")
    b = 0.35
    prev = None
    for xi in [0.35, 0.45, 0.60, 0.90, 1.40, 2.10]:
        v = gauss_transfer(s, b, xi)
        flag = "" if prev is None else ("  strictly smaller" if v < prev else "  !! NOT monotone")
        print(f"    xi = {xi:5.2f}   |F| = {v:.8f}{flag}")
        prev = v
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Windowed statistics, false nulls, and the scale space
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def window_sum_rect(ordinates: Sequence[float], T: float) -> float:
    """Sharp cutoff statistic: sum over |t| <= T of 1/(1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates if abs(t) <= T)


def gauss_spectral(ordinates: Sequence[float], s: float) -> float:
    """Gaussian scale space Sigma(S, s) = sum_t g_s(t) / (1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(gauss_window(s, t) / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


def harmonic_statistic(ordinates: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Unwindowed statistic sum_t 1/(1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


# The first few ordinates of the classical critical-line family, used as realistic data.
ORDINATES: List[float] = [14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062,
                          37.586178, 40.918719, 43.327073, 48.005151, 49.773832]


def demo_scale_space() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5. NO FALSE NULLS, AND THE GAUSSIAN SCALE SPACE")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("  Rectangular cutoff on the first ten ordinates (it jumps, and vanishes early):")
    for T in [5.0, 14.0, 14.134725, 20.0, 21.022040, 100.0]:
        print(f"    T = {T:10.6f}   windowSum = {window_sum_rect(ORDINATES, T):.8f}")
    print()
    print("  Gaussian scale space (continuous, strictly increasing, never zero):")
    prev = None
    for s in [1.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0, 80.0, 200.0, 1000.0]:
        v = gauss_spectral(ORDINATES, s)
        mono = "" if prev is None else ("  increasing" if v > prev else "  !! NOT increasing")
        print(f"    s = {s:8.1f}   Sigma = {v:.6e}{mono}")
        prev = v
    print(f"  unwindowed limit  sum 1/(1/4 + t^2) = {harmonic_statistic(ORDINATES):.6e}")
    print()
    print("  A single ordinate outside the cutoff is invisible to the sharp window:")
    t_far = 21.02204
    print(f"    windowSum({{{t_far}}}, T = 10) = {window_sum_rect([t_far], 10.0):.10f}")
    for s in [10.0, 20.0, 50.0]:
        print(f"    Gaussian statistic, s = {s:4.1f}   = {gauss_spectral([t_far], s):.3e}  (> 0)")
    # For very narrow windows the value is still strictly positive but underflows binary
    # floating point; its base-10 logarithm is computed exactly instead.
    for s in [0.5, 2.0]:
        log10_val = (-math.pi * t_far * t_far / (s * s)) / math.log(10.0) \
            - math.log10(0.25 + t_far * t_far)
        print(f"    Gaussian statistic, s = {s:4.1f}   = 10^({log10_val:.1f})  (> 0, underflows float)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Peak localisation and the Rayleigh criterion
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pos_profile(ordinates: Sequence[float], s: float, a: float) -> float:
    """Position profile P_S(a) = sum_t g_s(t - a) / (1/4 + t^2)."""
    return sum(gauss_window(s, t - a) / (0.25 + t * t) for t in ordinates)


def rayleigh_resolved(t1: float, t2: float, s: float) -> bool:
    """Rayleigh criterion 3 g_{2s}(t1 - t2) (1/4 + t1^2) <= 1/4 + t2^2."""
    return 3.0 * gauss_window(2.0 * s, t1 - t2) * (0.25 + t1 * t1) <= 0.25 + t2 * t2


def demo_peaks() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6. PEAK LOCALISATION AND THE RAYLEIGH CRITERION")
    print("=" * 78)
    t1, t2 = 14.134725, 21.022040
    for s in [10.0, 6.0, 4.0, 2.0]:
        u = gauss_window(2.0 * s, t1 - t2)
        w1, w2 = 1.0 / (0.25 + t1 * t1), 1.0 / (0.25 + t2 * t2)
        at_t1 = pos_profile([t1, t2], s, t1)
        at_mid = pos_profile([t1, t2], s, (t1 + t2) / 2.0)
        # Exact values from the scale-doubling identities.
        pred_t1 = w1 + u ** 4 * w2
        pred_mid = u * (w1 + w2)
        # Exact factorisation of the difference.
        factored = (1.0 - u) * (w1 - u * (1.0 + u + u * u) * w2)
        print(f"  s = {s:5.1f}:  u = g_2s(d) = {u:.6f}")
        print(f"      P(t1)      = {at_t1:.10f}   (formula w1 + u^4 w2 = {pred_t1:.10f})")
        print(f"      P(midpoint)= {at_mid:.10f}   (formula u(w1 + w2)  = {pred_mid:.10f})")
        print(f"      difference = {at_t1 - at_mid:.10f}   "
              f"(factorisation (1-u)(w1 - u(1+u+u^2)w2) = {factored:.10f})")
        print(f"      sharp criterion u(1+u+u^2)w2 < w1 : "
              f"{u * (1 + u + u * u) * w2:.3e} < {w1:.3e}  -> "
              f"{'RESOLVED' if u * (1 + u + u * u) * w2 < w1 else 'merged'}")
        print(f"      Rayleigh criterion (constant 3)   : "
              f"{'satisfied' if rayleigh_resolved(t1, t2, s) else 'not satisfied'}")
    print()
    print("  Unbiased localisation for a single ordinate (peak exactly at t):")
    t = 14.134725
    for a in [t - 1.0, t - 0.1, t, t + 0.1, t + 1.0]:
        print(f"    a = {a:11.6f}   P(a) = {pos_profile([t], 3.0, a):.10f}")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Schwartz bounds and regularisation
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def schwartz_bound(s: float, n: int) -> float:
    """The explicit constant (s^2/pi)^n n! in (t^2)^n g_s(t) <= (s^2/pi)^n n!."""
    return (s * s / math.pi) ** n * math.factorial(n)


def demo_schwartz() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7. EXPLICIT SCHWARTZ BOUNDS AND GAUSSIAN REGULARISATION")
    print("=" * 78)
    s = 1.0
    print(f"  Checking (t^2)^n g_s(t) <= (s^2/pi)^n n!   for s = {s}:")
    for n in [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]:
        bound = schwartz_bound(s, n)
        worst = max(((t * t) ** n) * gauss_window(s, t)
                    for t in [i * 0.01 for i in range(0, 2001)])
        ok = "ok" if worst <= bound + 1e-9 else "VIOLATED"
        print(f"    n = {n}:  max_t (t^2)^n g_s(t) = {worst:12.6f} <= {bound:12.6f}   [{ok}]")
    print()
    print("  Regularisation on the threshold family t_k = sqrt(k+1):")
    unwindowed = 0.0
    windowed = 0.0
    checkpoints = {3, 10, 100, 1000, 10000}
    for k in range(10000):
        tk2 = float(k + 1)
        unwindowed += 1.0 / (0.25 + tk2)
        windowed += gauss_window(s, math.sqrt(tk2)) / (0.25 + tk2)
        if k + 1 in checkpoints:
            print(f"    k < {k + 1:6d}:  unwindowed = {unwindowed:10.6f}   "
                  f"Gaussian-windowed = {windowed:.8f}")
    print("    the unwindowed partial sums grow like log k (divergent harmonic series),")
    print("    while the Gaussian-windowed sum is constant to five digits past k = 3.")
    print()
    print("  Uniform decay over the Heisenberg orbit, |t-a|^m |gamma_{s,a,b}(t)| <= 1 + (s^2/pi)^m m!:")
    m = 2
    bound = 1.0 + schwartz_bound(s, m)
    worst = 0.0
    for a in [-3.0, 0.0, 1.7]:
        for b in [-2.0, 0.0, 5.0]:
            atom = gabor_atom(s, a, b)
            for i in range(0, 1200):
                t = a - 6.0 + i * 0.01
                worst = max(worst, abs(t - a) ** m * abs(atom(t)))
    print(f"    m = {m}: worst value over a grid of (a, b, t) = {worst:.6f} <= {bound:.6f}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_weyl_relation()
    demo_heisenberg()
    demo_sidelobes()
    demo_scale_space()
    demo_peaks()
    demo_schwartz()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("All demonstrations completed.")
    print("=" * 78)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Tuple

TAU: float = 2.0 * math.pi


def rect_transfer_abs(T: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F 1_[-T,T](xi)| = |sin(2 pi T xi)| / (pi |xi|); the value at xi = 0 is 2T."""
    if xi == 0.0:
        return 2.0 * T
    return abs(math.sin(TAU * T * xi)) / (math.pi * abs(xi))


def gauss_transfer_abs(s: float, xi: float) -> float:
    """|F gamma_{s,a,0}(xi)| = s exp(-pi s^2 xi^2), independent of the position a."""
    return s * math.exp(-math.pi * s * s * xi * xi)


def sidelobe_freq(T: float, n: int) -> float:
    """The n-th sidelobe frequency xi_n = (2n+1)/(4T)."""
    return (2.0 * n + 1.0) / (4.0 * T)


def leakage_table(T: float, s: float, orders: List[int]) -> List[Tuple[int, float, float, float, float]]:
    """Rows (n, xi_n, |F rect|, normalised amplitude, |F gauss|)."""
    rows: List[Tuple[int, float, float, float, float]] = []
    for n in orders:
        xi = sidelobe_freq(T, n)
        r = rect_transfer_abs(T, xi)
        rows.append((n, xi, r, xi * r, gauss_transfer_abs(s, xi)))
    return rows


def partial_energy(T: float, s: float, terms: int) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Partial sums of the sidelobe amplitudes for both windows."""
    rect = sum(rect_transfer_abs(T, sidelobe_freq(T, n)) for n in range(terms))
    gauss = sum(gauss_transfer_abs(s, sidelobe_freq(T, n)) for n in range(terms))
    return rect, gauss


def main() -> None:
    s = 1.0
    for T in (0.5, 2.0, 10.0):
        print(f"--- rectangular half-width T = {T}, Gaussian width s = {s} ---")
        print("    n      xi_n     |F rect|   xi_n |F rect|      |F gauss|")
        for n, xi, r, norm, g in leakage_table(T, s, [0, 1, 2, 5, 20, 100]):
            exact = 4.0 * T / (math.pi * (2.0 * n + 1.0))
            assert abs(r - exact) < 1e-12
            print(f"  {n:4d} {xi:9.4f} {r:12.6f} {norm:14.9f} {g:15.4e}")
        for terms in (10, 1000, 100000):
            rect, gauss = partial_energy(T, s, terms)
            print(f"  partial sums over {terms:6d} sidelobes:"
                  f"  rectangular = {rect:9.4f}   Gaussian = {gauss:.10f}")
        print()
    print("The normalised amplitude column is identically 1/pi = "
          f"{1.0 / math.pi:.9f}: it depends on neither n nor T.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def gauss_window(s: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Gaussian window g_s(t) = exp(-pi t^2 / s^2)."""
    return math.exp(-math.pi * t * t / (s * s))


def position_profile(data: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]], s: float, a: float) -> float:
    """Slide the width-s Gaussian to position a: P(a) = sum_j w_j g_s(t_j - a)."""
    return sum(w * gauss_window(s, t - a) for t, w in data)


def scale_space(data: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]], widths: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """The monotone, continuous curve s -> P(0) evaluated at the requested widths."""
    return [position_profile(data, s, 0.0) for s in widths]


def local_maxima(grid: Sequence[float], values: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Interior grid points whose value strictly exceeds both neighbours."""
    return [grid[i] for i in range(1, len(values) - 1)
            if values[i] > values[i - 1] and values[i] > values[i + 1]]


def rayleigh_resolved(t1: float, w1: float, t2: float, w2: float, s: float) -> bool:
    """Sharp criterion u(1 + u + u^2) w2 < w1 with u = g_{2s}(t1 - t2)."""
    u = gauss_window(2.0 * s, t1 - t2)
    return u * (1.0 + u + u * u) * w2 < w1


def all_pairs_certified(peaks: Sequence[float],
                        amplitudes: Sequence[float],
                        s: float) -> bool:
    """Every adjacent pair of peaks must be resolved in both directions."""
    return all(
        rayleigh_resolved(peaks[i], amplitudes[i], peaks[i + 1], amplitudes[i + 1], s)
        and rayleigh_resolved(peaks[i + 1], amplitudes[i + 1], peaks[i], amplitudes[i], s)
        for i in range(len(peaks) - 1)

def find_peaks(data: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]],
               s0: float,
               grid_lo: float,
               grid_hi: float,
               grid_n: int = 4001,
               max_refinements: int = 20,
               shrink: float = 0.75) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Sweep widths downward from s0 and return the widest certified peak list.

    Complexity: O(max_refinements * grid_n * |data|) window evaluations.
    """
    grid: List[float] = [grid_lo + (grid_hi - grid_lo) * i / (grid_n - 1)
                         for i in range(grid_n)]
    best: Dict[str, object] = {"width": s0, "peaks": [], "rounds": 0, "certified": False}
    s = s0

        values = [position_profile(data, s, a) for a in grid]
        peaks = local_maxima(grid, values)
        amplitudes = [position_profile(data, s, p) for p in peaks]
        if peaks and all_pairs_certified(peaks, amplitudes, s):
            if len(peaks) > len(best["peaks"]):  # type: ignore[arg-type]
                best = {"width": s, "peaks": peaks,
                        "rounds": round_index + 1, "certified": True}

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

TAU: float = 2.0 * math.pi
Datum = Tuple[float, complex]
Window = Callable[[float], complex]


def chi(x: float) -> complex:
    """The additive character chi(x) = exp(2 pi i x)."""
    return cmath.exp(1j * TAU * x)


def gaussian_window(s: float) -> Window:
    """The analysing window g_s(t) = exp(-pi t^2 / s^2), as a complex-valued function."""
    return lambda t: complex(math.exp(-math.pi * t * t / (s * s)), 0.0)


def gabor_transform(data: Sequence[Datum], w: Window, a: float, b: float) -> complex:
    """G_w(D)(a, b): analyse the phase-space point (position a, frequency b)."""
    return sum(chi(-b * t) * w(t - a) * c for t, c in data)


def translate_data(data: Sequence[Datum], c: float) -> List[Datum]:
    """Shift every ordinate by c."""
    return [(t + c, amp) for t, amp in data]


def modulate_data(data: Sequence[Datum], eta: float) -> List[Datum]:
    """Multiply every amplitude by the character chi(eta t)."""
    return [(t, chi(eta * t) * amp) for t, amp in data]


def weyl_phase(eta: float, c: float) -> complex:
    """The phase chi(-eta c) relating the two orders of translation and modulation."""
    return chi(-eta * c)


def transform_after_motions(data: Sequence[Datum], w: Window, a: float, b: float,
                            c: float, eta: float, modulate_first: bool) -> complex:
    """Apply both motions in the chosen order and analyse the result."""
    moved = translate_data(modulate_data(data, eta), c) if modulate_first \
        else modulate_data(translate_data(data, c), eta)
    return gabor_transform(moved, w, a, b)

                               c: float, eta: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:

    first = transform_after_motions(data, w, a, b, c, eta, modulate_first=True)
    second = transform_after_motions(data, w, a, b, c, eta, modulate_first=False)
    return abs(first - weyl_phase(eta, c) * second), abs(first - second)

    return math.exp(-math.pi * t * t / (s * s))

    """C_n = (s^2 / pi)^n n!, the constant in (t^2)^n g_s(t) <= C_n."""
    return (s * s / math.pi) ** n * math.factorial(n)

  "interactive_layout": "# Smooth Windows — a guided tour

*Every measurement of a spectrum looks at an infinite object through a finite aperture. This page
is about the shape of that aperture: why the obvious choice is the worst one, what the right one
is, and why the reason is ultimately algebraic rather than analytic.*

---

## 1. The window you didn't know you chose

Suppose your data are a family of *ordinates* $t$ — heights along a line — each carrying a weight
$w_t$, and you want the total $\sum_t w_t$. You cannot sum infinitely many terms, so you keep the
ones with $|t| \le T$ and discard the rest. That is a choice of window:

$$\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}(t) = \begin{cases}1 & |t|\le T\\ 0 & |t|>T\end{cases}$$

It feels neutral — take everything, weight it equally, decide nothing. It is not neutral. This
page shows it has three specific, quantifiable defects, and that a single alternative repairs all
three.

> **The alternative.** The **Gaussian window** of width $s$:
> $$g_s(t) = e^{-\pi t^2/s^2}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Why write the Gaussian with a $\pi$ in the exponent?</b></summary>

With the convention $\widehat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2\pi i \xi t} f(t)\,dt$ for the
[Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform), the normalisation
$g_s(t)=e^{-\pi t^2/s^2}$ makes the self-duality statement perfectly clean:

$$\widehat{g_s} = s\,g_{1/s}.$$

No stray factors of $\sqrt{2\pi}$. The width simply inverts, which is the
[uncertainty principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty_principle) for this family
written as an identity rather than an inequality.
</details>

---

## 2. Defect one: the sharp window rings forever

Multiplying data by a window in one variable smears the spectrum by the window's Fourier
transform — its **transfer function** — in the other. For the rectangle this is the
[Dirichlet kernel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_kernel):

$$\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi) = \frac{\sin(2\pi T\xi)}{\pi\xi}, \qquad \xi \ne 0.$$

It has a tall central lobe — the part you wanted — and then oscillates forever with a slowly
decaying envelope. Those oscillations are **sidelobes**: energy from distant frequencies leaking
into your local measurement, and structure your peak finder may report as real.

Play with the widths below. Whatever you do to $T$, the orange dots keep touching the same
envelope, and the readout keeps reporting the same number.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

The number is not an accident. The sidelobe peaks sit at $\xi_n = (2n+1)/(4T)$ with exact height
$4T/(\pi(2n+1))$, so

$$\xi_n \cdot \bigl|\widehat{\mathbf{1}_{[-T,T]}}(\xi_n)\bigr| = \frac{1}{\pi}
\qquad\text{for every } n \text{ and every } T.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the computation</b></summary>

The indicator integral is elementary:
$$\int_{-T}^{T} e^{-2\pi i\xi t}\,dt = \frac{e^{-2\pi i\xi T}-e^{2\pi i \xi T}}{-2\pi i\xi}
= \frac{\sin(2\pi T\xi)}{\pi\xi}.$$
At $\xi_n=(2n+1)/(4T)$ we have $2\pi T\xi_n = (2n+1)\pi/2$, so $|\sin(2\pi T \xi_n)| = 1$ and the
modulus is $1/(\pi\xi_n) = 4T/(\pi(2n+1))$. Multiplying by $\xi_n$ cancels everything and leaves
$1/\pi$. (At $\xi=0$ the transfer function equals $2T$, not $0/0$ — that case must be excluded.)
</details>

Two consequences. There is **no** bound of the form $|\widehat{\mathbf 1}_{[-T,T]}(\xi)|=o(1/\xi)$,
since the normalised amplitude hits $1/\pi$ infinitely often. And the amplitudes
$4T/(\pi(2n+1))$ form a **divergent** series: the total spurious energy of a sharp cutoff is
infinite.

The Gaussian has none of this. Its Gabor atom — a Gaussian bump at position $a$ vibrating at
frequency $b$, $\gamma_{s,a,b}(t) = e^{2\pi i b(t-a)}g_s(t-a)$ — has transfer modulus

$$\bigl|\widehat{\gamma_{s,a,b}}(\xi)\bigr| = s\,g_{1/s}(\xi-b):$$

a single lobe, strictly decreasing in $|\xi - b|$, decaying faster than every power of $\xi$, and
with **summable** responses at the very frequencies where the rectangle leaks.

{{visualization:0}}

{{demo:1}}

---

## 3. What must not break: the Weyl relation

Smoothing would be worthless if it broke the bookkeeping. A window is not a static object: you
slide it and you tune it. Those two motions are

$$(T_a f)(t) = f(t-a), \qquad (M_b f)(t) = e^{2\pi i bt}f(t),$$

and the central question is whether they commute. Almost — and the "almost" is the whole story:

$$\boxed{\,M_b T_a = e^{2\pi i ab}\; T_a M_b\,}$$

Turn the dial and watch the two composites, as vectors in the complex plane. Same length always;
same direction only when $ab$ is a whole number.

{{interactive_demo:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the one-line proof, and why the phase is unremovable</b></summary>

Evaluate at $t$. The left side is $e^{2\pi ibt}f(t-a)$. The right side is
$e^{2\pi iab}\,e^{2\pi i b(t-a)}f(t-a)$, and the two exponents add to $2\pi i bt$. Done.

That the phase is real, and not an artefact of a bad convention, is settled by one example: take
$a=b=\tfrac12$ and evaluate at $t=\tfrac12$. Then $M_bT_af(\tfrac12) = i\,f(0)$ while
$T_aM_bf(\tfrac12) = f(0)$. For any window with $f(0)\ne 0$ the two orders genuinely differ.
</details>

The failure to commute is the good kind of failure, because there is a group behind it. Bundle a
translation, a modulation and a unimodular phase into a triple and multiply by

$$(a,b,z)\cdot(a',b',z') = \bigl(a+a',\;b+b',\;zz'e^{2\pi i ba'}\bigr).$$

This is the [Heisenberg group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisenberg_group), and the assignment
$(a,b,z)\mapsto z\,T_aM_b$ — the **Schrödinger**, or **Gabor**, **representation** — is an exact
homomorphism: the composite of two Gabor shifts is a third one, with no error term.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the group law is exactly the Weyl phase, and why a single Gaussian proves faithfulness</b></summary>

Associativity of that multiplication is equivalent to the polynomial identity
$$b a' + (b+b')a'' = b'a'' + b(a'+a''),$$
the 2-cocycle condition for the Weyl phase. The group exists *because* the relation holds.

Faithfulness is proved with one test vector, the Gaussian $\gamma(t)=e^{-t^2}$. Suppose
$z\,T_aM_b$ fixes it.
1. Take absolute values: this kills $z$ and the character, leaving $e^{-(t-a)^2}=e^{-t^2}$.
   The Gaussian has a unique maximum, so $a = 0$.
2. Now $z\,e^{2\pi i bt}\gamma(t)=\gamma(t)$, and $\gamma$ is nowhere zero, so
   $z\,e^{2\pi ibt}=1$ for all $t$. At $t=0$: $z=1$.
3. So $e^{2\pi ibt}=1$ for all $t$. If $b\ne0$, take $t=1/(4b)$: this says $i = 1$. So $b=0$.

Consequence: the central circle is not redundant, the phase cannot be rescaled away, and the
Gaussian is already distinguished before a single analytic estimate is made.
</details>

The Gaussian sits inside this structure perfectly: the group merely permutes the Gabor atoms,
carrying the atom at $(a,b)$ to the atom at $(a_0+a,\,b_0+b)$ and changing nothing but a phase.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 4. Defect two: false nulls and jumps

Now put the machinery to work. Suppose the ordinates come in conjugate pairs, contributing
$1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$ each, and consider the windowed statistic

$$\Sigma(S,s) = \sum_{t \in S} \frac{g_s(t)}{\tfrac14 + t^2}.$$

Taking the rectangular window instead recovers the classical sharp cutoff exactly, so this is a
strict generalisation, not a change of subject.

* **The sharp cutoff can be blind.** It returns $0$ for every $T$ below the first ordinate — the
  same answer it gives for no data at all. A pair of zeros with $|t| > T$ is completely invisible.
* **The Gaussian never is.** Being strictly positive everywhere, it returns a strictly positive
  number for every nonempty family at every width, and $0$ only for the empty family.
* **The sharp cutoff jumps.** As $T$ crosses $|t|$ the statistic leaps by exactly
  $1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$. The Gaussian statistic is continuous in the width, non-decreasing, strictly
  increasing whenever a nonzero ordinate is present, and converges as $s\to\infty$ to the full
  unwindowed sum $\sum_t 1/(\tfrac14+t^2)$.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly: **positivity** of the window removes false nulls;
**smoothness** removes sidelobes. Two independent defects, one window that fixes both.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 5. Defect three: resolution

Slide the window instead of just widening it, and record the **position profile**

$$P_S(a) = \sum_{t\in S} \frac{g_s(t-a)}{\tfrac14+t^2}.$$

For a single ordinate this has a strict global maximum exactly at that ordinate: a Gaussian window
never displaces a peak. For two ordinates, the question "two peaks or one?" has a closed-form
answer, and it lives in a single variable.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the factorisation behind the verdict</b></summary>

The Gaussian satisfies two *scale-doubling identities*:
$$g_s(d/2) = g_{2s}(d), \qquad g_s(d) = g_{2s}(d)^4.$$
Set $u = g_{2s}(t_1-t_2)$ and $w_i = 1/(\tfrac14+t_i^2)$. Then the profile at the far ordinate
and at the midpoint are
$$P(t_1) = w_1 + u^4 w_2, \qquad P\!\left(\tfrac{t_1+t_2}{2}\right) = u(w_1+w_2),$$
so, using $1-u^3=(1-u)(1+u+u^2)$,
$$P(t_1) - P\!\left(\tfrac{t_1+t_2}{2}\right) = (1-u)\bigl(w_1 - u(1+u+u^2)w_2\bigr).$$

Two factors, two failure modes, cleanly separated. The first vanishes exactly when $u=1$, i.e.
when the two ordinates coincide. The second is the genuine threshold: the peaks are resolved iff
$u(1+u+u^2)w_2 < w_1$. Bounding $1+u+u^2<3$ gives the usable
[Rayleigh-type criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_resolution)
$$3\,g_{2s}(t_1-t_2)\bigl(\tfrac14+t_1^2\bigr) \le \tfrac14+t_2^2 .$$

And since $g_{2s}(d)\to0$ as $s\downarrow 0$ for any fixed $d\ne0$, **any** two distinct ordinates
are resolved by all sufficiently narrow windows. There is no resolution floor — unlike the
rectangle, whose relative sidelobe height is the width-independent $1/\pi$.
</details>

That criterion is exactly what turns a peak finder into a *certified* peak finder: detect maxima,
then check each adjacent pair, and narrow the window until every check passes.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 6. A window that creates convergence

The last surprise is that a smooth window is not merely a better sharp window. It can make sense
of data the sharp window cannot even parse.

The Gaussian's decay is explicit and quantitative: for every order $n$ and every $t$,

$$(t^2)^n\,g_s(t) \;\le\; \left(\frac{s^2}{\pi}\right)^{\!n} n! .$$

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof — it is one substitution</b></summary>

Put $y = \pi t^2/s^2 \ge 0$, so $g_s(t)=e^{-y}$ and $t^2 = (s^2/\pi)y$. The exponential series
gives $y^n/n! \le e^y$, hence $y^n e^{-y}\le n!$. Multiply by $(s^2/\pi)^n$.

Two features matter. The constant is **independent of $t$**, so you may choose the order $n$
*after* seeing how fast your data grow. And the same bound holds uniformly across the entire
Heisenberg orbit: every Gabor atom obeys $|t-a|^m|\gamma_{s,a,b}(t)| \le 1 + (s^2/\pi)^m m!$ with a
constant that does not depend on the phase-space point $(a,b)$.
</details>

Take an infinite family of ordinates growing only as fast as $t_k^2 \ge k+1$. Then the
Gaussian-windowed series $\sum_k g_s(t_k)/(\tfrac14+t_k^2)$ converges absolutely — already at
$n=2$ the terms are $O(1/k^2)$. But on the threshold family $t_k=\sqrt{k+1}$ the *unwindowed*
series is $\sum_k 1/(k+\tfrac54)$: the harmonic series, divergent.

{{algorithm:2}}

With $s=1$: the unwindowed partial sums crawl past $9.4$ by $k=10^4$ and keep climbing like
$\log k$, while the Gaussian-windowed sum settles at $\approx 0.0354$ and is constant to five
digits after $k=3$. No window bounded below by a positive constant can do this — and a rectangular
window of infinite width is exactly the unwindowed sum.

---

## 7. Everything at once

The full battery of checks, in one run: the Weyl relation and the Heisenberg group law, the exact
sidelobe amplitudes, the strictly unimodal Gaussian transfer function, the scale space and its
wide-window limit, the profile factorisation and the Rayleigh verdict, and the regularisation of a
divergent statistic.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 8. The moral

There is no neutral window. The sharp cutoff is a very particular choice with three signatures:
infinite spurious energy at the fixed relative amplitude $1/\pi$, a statistic that jumps and can
vanish while data are present, and a resolution floor that never improves.

The Gaussian is a different particular choice, and it is the right one for a reason that is
finally algebraic. It is the fixed family of the Fourier transform, so its transfer function is a
single unimodal bump. It is nowhere zero, so it invents no false nulls. It decays faster than any
polynomial with explicit constants, so it regularises. And it sits inside a faithful representation
of the Heisenberg group that permutes its translates and modulates exactly, so every one of those
properties holds uniformly as the window is slid and tuned across phase space.

When you choose a window, you are choosing a vector in a representation space, and the group acting
on it does not care whether you noticed. The only question is whether your vector is a good one.

namespace SmoothWindows

open Complex Real ReciprocalZeroHarmonics

/-- The **Gaussian spectral profile** of a family of critical-line ordinates:
`Σ_t g_s(t)/(1/4 + t²)`. -/
noncomputable def gaussSpectral (S : Multiset ℝ) (s : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (S.map fun t => gaussWin s t / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2)).sum

@[simp] theorem gaussSpectral_zero (s : ℝ) : gaussSpectral 0 s = 0 := by simp [gaussSpectral]

@[simp] theorem gaussSpectral_cons (t : ℝ) (S : Multiset ℝ) (s : ℝ) :
    gaussSpectral (t ::ₘ S) s = gaussWin s t / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2) + gaussSpectral S s := by
  simp [gaussSpectral]

/-- The spectral profile is the real part of the Gaussian-windowed harmonic sum. -/
theorem gaussSum_pairedOrdinates_re (S : Multiset ℝ) (s : ℝ) :
    (gaussSum (pairedOrdinates S) s).re = gaussSpectral S s := by
  rw [gaussSum_pairedOrdinates, Complex.ofReal_re, gaussSpectral]

/-! ## Monotonicity in the window width -/

theorem gaussWin_le_of_le {s₁ s₂ : ℝ} (h1 : 0 < s₁) (h : s₁ ≤ s₂) (t : ℝ) :
    gaussWin s₁ t ≤ gaussWin s₂ t := by
  rw [gaussWin, gaussWin, Real.exp_le_exp]
  have h1' : 0 < s₁ ^ 2 := pow_pos h1 2
  have h2' : 0 < s₂ ^ 2 := pow_pos (lt_of_lt_of_le h1 h) 2
  have hs : s₁ ^ 2 ≤ s₂ ^ 2 := by nlinarith
  rw [div_le_div_iff₀ h1' h2']
  nlinarith [mul_nonneg (mul_nonneg Real.pi_pos.le (sq_nonneg t)) (sub_nonneg.mpr hs)]

theorem gaussWin_lt_of_lt {t : ℝ} (ht : t ≠ 0) {s₁ s₂ : ℝ} (h1 : 0 < s₁) (h : s₁ < s₂) :
    gaussWin s₁ t < gaussWin s₂ t := by
  rw [gaussWin, gaussWin, Real.exp_lt_exp]
  have h1' : 0 < s₁ ^ 2 := pow_pos h1 2
  have h2' : 0 < s₂ ^ 2 := pow_pos (h1.trans h) 2
  have ht2 : 0 < t ^ 2 := lt_of_le_of_ne (sq_nonneg t) (Ne.symm (pow_ne_zero 2 ht))
  have hs : s₁ ^ 2 < s₂ ^ 2 := by nlinarith
  rw [div_lt_div_iff₀ h1' h2']
  nlinarith [mul_pos (mul_pos Real.pi_pos ht2) (sub_pos.mpr hs)]

/-- **Monotone scale space.**  Widening the Gaussian window never decreases the detected
spectral mass. -/
theorem gaussSpectral_mono (S : Multiset ℝ) {s₁ s₂ : ℝ} (h1 : 0 < s₁) (h : s₁ ≤ s₂) :
    gaussSpectral S s₁ ≤ gaussSpectral S s₂ := by
  refine Multiset.sum_map_le_sum_map _ _ fun t _ => ?_
  have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < 1 / 4 + t ^ 2 := by positivity
  have := gaussWin_le_of_le h1 h t
  gcongr

/-- **Strictly monotone scale space.**  If the family contains a nonzero ordinate the profile is
strictly increasing in the width. -/
theorem gaussSpectral_strictMono {S : Multiset ℝ} {t : ℝ} (ht : t ∈ S) (ht0 : t ≠ 0)
    {s₁ s₂ : ℝ} (h1 : 0 < s₁) (h : s₁ < s₂) :
    gaussSpectral S s₁ < gaussSpectral S s₂ := by
  obtain ⟨S', rfl⟩ := Multiset.exists_cons_of_mem ht
  rw [gaussSpectral_cons, gaussSpectral_cons]
  have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < 1 / 4 + t ^ 2 := by positivity
  have hstrict : gaussWin s₁ t / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2) < gaussWin s₂ t / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2) := by
    have := gaussWin_lt_of_lt ht0 h1 h
    gcongr
  have hrest : gaussSpectral S' s₁ ≤ gaussSpectral S' s₂ := gaussSpectral_mono S' h1 h.le
  linarith

/-! ## Continuity in the window width -/

/-- **The Gaussian scale space is continuous in the width.** -/
theorem gaussSpectral_continuousOn (S : Multiset ℝ) :
    ContinuousOn (fun s : ℝ => gaussSpectral S s) {s : ℝ | s ≠ 0} := by
  induction S using Multiset.induction_on with
  | empty => simpa using continuousOn_const
  | cons t S ih =>
    have harg : ContinuousOn (fun s : ℝ => -π * t ^ 2 / s ^ 2) {s : ℝ | s ≠ 0} :=
      continuousOn_const.div ((continuous_pow 2).continuousOn) fun s hs => pow_ne_zero 2 hs
    have hterm : ContinuousOn (fun s : ℝ => gaussWin s t / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2)) {s : ℝ | s ≠ 0} := by
      refine ContinuousOn.div_const ?_ _
      exact Real.continuous_exp.comp_continuousOn harg
    simpa using hterm.add ih

/-! ## The rectangular cutoff jumps -/

theorem windowSum_pairedOrdinates_singleton (t T : ℝ) :
    windowSum (pairedOrdinates {t}) T
      = if |t| ≤ T then ((1 / (1 / 4 + t ^ 2) : ℝ) : ℂ) else 0 := by
  classical
  rw [windowSum_pairedOrdinates]
  by_cases h : |t| ≤ T
  · rw [if_pos h, Multiset.filter_singleton, if_pos h, harmonicSum_pairedOrdinates]
    simp
  · rw [if_neg h, Multiset.filter_singleton, if_neg h]

/-! ## The character `χ(x) = e^{2πix}` -/

/-- The basic additive character `χ(x) = e^{2πix}` of `ℝ`. -/
noncomputable def chi (x : ℝ) : ℂ := Complex.exp ((2 * π * x : ℝ) * Complex.I)

@[simp] theorem chi_zero : chi 0 = 1 := by simp [chi]

theorem chi_add (x y : ℝ) : chi (x + y) = chi x * chi y := by
  unfold chi
  rw [← Complex.exp_add]
  push_cast
  ring_nf

@[simp] theorem chi_ne_zero (x : ℝ) : chi x ≠ 0 := Complex.exp_ne_zero _

@[simp] theorem norm_chi (x : ℝ) : ‖chi x‖ = 1 := by

  exact Complex.norm_exp_ofReal_mul_I (2 * π * x)

  rw [← chi_add]
  simp

  · rintro ⟨n, rfl⟩

/-! ## Translation and modulation -/

/-- **Translation** `(T_a f)(t) = f (t - a)`. -/
def transOp (a : ℝ) (f : ℝ → ℂ) : ℝ → ℂ := fun t => f (t - a)

/-- **Modulation** `(M_b f)(t) = e^{2πi b t} f (t)`. -/

@[simp] theorem transOp_zero (f : ℝ → ℂ) : transOp 0 f = f := by
  funext t; simp [transOp]

@[simp] theorem modOp_zero (f : ℝ → ℂ) : modOp 0 f = f := by
  funext t; simp [modOp]

theorem transOp_transOp (a a' : ℝ) (f : ℝ → ℂ) :
    transOp a (transOp a' f) = transOp (a + a') f := by

  simp only [modOp, ← mul_assoc, ← chi_add]
  ring_nf

/-- Translation and modulation are `ℂ`-linear in the window. -/
theorem transOp_add (a : ℝ) (f g : ℝ → ℂ) :

theorem modOp_add (b : ℝ) (f g : ℝ → ℂ) :
    modOp b (f + g) = modOp b f + modOp b g := by
  funext t; simp [modOp, mul_add]

/-- **The modulation/translation identity (Weyl commutation relation).**

  ring_nf

  rw [show -(b * a) + b * a = 0 by ring, chi_zero, one_mul]
